data.reason:
An adversarial multi-agent audit of the schema alone, run because three Codex rounds had died on a usage limit and the question worth answering was whether the schema is sound rather than whether the guards are. 135 agents across eight attack dimensions, every finding put to three independent refuters with distinct lenses and defaulting to refuted when uncertain, then a completeness critic over what the eight had not looked at. 42 findings attacked, 8 survived, and the critic found 4 more.

These are schema defects and not the guard prose the last five review rounds produced, and the reason they were not found earlier is that every one of those rounds was attacking the guards. The audit was told the guards were out of scope and to return empty if that was all it could find.

The two highs bear directly on ingest and on criterion 4. marketplace is bare text not null on the five tables criterion 4 names, with no foreign key, no check and no domain, while its own column comment says it is one of the six identifiers the catalogue defines. So the unique index on (tenant_id, marketplace, external_id) is an idempotency key only while the speller is consistent: 'bol', 'BOL' and 'not-a-marketplace' coexist with one external id, and a connector that changes its spelling doubles the trade record. The same column need not agree with the parent it hangs from, so an order carrying amazon sits on a bol connection. And order_lines carries no uniqueness on its marketplace line id at all, so re-ingesting one order duplicates every line and no upsert is possible, which is SEEN-014 broken before it is written.

The mediums extend the same class: the tenant travels along every key but the order does not, so a return's line may belong to another order and a settlement line may match an order line on another marketplace, which SEEN-018 will store and SEEN-019 and SEEN-020 will then read as truth. Three externally sourced tables carry a marketplace id with no unique index. The seeded Bol correspondence capability disagrees with the routing table.

The critic's four are evidence and billing: erasing a tenant deletes the pointer to its evidence and leaves the bytes in the bucket with the only tenant mapping destroyed by the same statement; evidence.storage_path is free text with no relation to its own tenant_id; connections_marketplace_fkey cascades on both columns of its key; and invoices.recovery_share_lines is untyped jsonb, so the billable chain has no last hop.

What the audit ruled out by measurement is worth recording beside what it found: no view or materialised view in public, every seen function with an empty search_path and only current_tenant reachable, every temporal column timestamptz, every cents column bigint, external_id not null on all five tables, no partial or expression unique index, no NOT VALID or DEFERRABLE constraint, the eight set-null keys all in the column-list form, anon holding nothing, and criterion 3 failing closed on both a missing claim and a malformed one.

findings.file: public.orders.marketplace, shipments.marketplace, returns.marketplace, settlements.marketplace, settlement_lines.marketplace, claims.marketplace — /Users/ruudvanengelenhoven/Development/seene/supabase/migrations/20260927000000_trade_record_v1_tenancy_and_orders.sql:160,175,234,266,302,341,363 and un
findings.claim: marketplace is unconstrained free text, so the criterion-4 unique key is bypassed by any spelling and a child may name a marketplace its parent does not
findings.failure_scenario:
The column comment on public.orders.marketplace says 'One of the six identifiers the marketplaces catalogue defines', but only connections.marketplace has a foreign key to public.marketplaces. On the five tables criterion 4 names, plus claims, marketplace is bare `text not null` with no FK, no check constraint and no domain. Two consequences, both demonstrated. First, the unique index on (tenant_id, marketplace, external_id) is only an idempotency key while marketplace is written identically: the same external order id ingests again under 'BOL' or 'not-a-marketplace' and both rows survive, so a connector that changes its spelling silently doubles the trade record. Second, the marketplace does not have to agree with the parent the row hangs from: an order carrying marketplace='amazon' sits happily on a bol connection, and two shipments with the same external id but different marketplace values hang off one bol order.

MEASURED:
(a) INSERT 0 1 three times, no error:
    marketplace    | external_id 
-------------------+-------------
 bol               | ORD-1
 BOL               | ORD-1
 not-a-marketplace | ORD-1
(3 rows)

(b) accepted:
 external_id | order_mkt | conn_mkt 
-------------+-----------+----------
 ORD-1       | amazon    | bol
(1 row)

(c) accepted:
 shipments_for_one_bol_order 
-----------------------------
                           2
(1 row)

For contrast the key itself does work when marketplace is written the same way: a fourth insert of ('bol','ORD-1') gives `ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "orders_tenant_marketplace_external_id_key"`.

findings.file: public.returns_order_line_id_fkey and public.settlement_lines_order_line_id_fkey — /Users/ruudvanengelenhoven/Development/seene/supabase/migrations/20260929000000_trade_record_v1_tenant_scoped_foreign_keys.sql (the rewrite list, returns/order_line_id and settlement_lines/order_line_id)
findings.claim: The tenant travels along every key but the order does not: a return's line may belong to another order, and a settlement line may match an order line on another marketplace
findings.failure_scenario:
Part 5 rewrote every key as (tenant_id, child_id) references parent (tenant_id, id), which closes the cross-tenant edge and does so correctly: all 27 cross-tenant inserts I attempted were refused with 23503, and erasing one tenant destroyed exactly its own rows and left the other's intact. What the rewrite does not close is the case where a row has two parents that must agree. returns carries both order_id and order_line_id, and nothing requires the line to be a line of that order. settlement_lines carries both settlement_id and order_line_id, and nothing requires the matched order line to sit under an order on the same connection or even the same marketplace as the settlement. SEEN-018 matches settlement lines to order lines deterministically and SEEN-019/SEEN-020 detect fee and return shortfalls from those joins; the database will store a match the detectors then read as truth. The fix is the same technique part 5 already paid for: carry order_id into the key the way tenant_id was carried, via a unique constraint on order_lines (tenant_id, order_id, id).

MEASURED:
Both accepted:
 external_id |             return_says              |           line_belongs_to            
-------------+--------------------------------------+--------------------------------------
 RET-1       | 01000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001 | 01000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000002
(1 row)

 line_mkt | matched_order_mkt 
----------+-------------------
 bol      | amazon
(1 row)

A settlement line may also disagree with its own settlement's marketplace: inserting a line with marketplace='amazon' under a settlement with marketplace='bol' is accepted and returns line_mkt=amazon, settlement_mkt=bol.

findings.file: /Users/ruudvanengelenhoven/Development/seene/supabase/migrations/20260927000000_trade_record_v1_tenancy_and_orders.sql:234 (public.orders.marketplace, and the same column on shipments, returns, settlements, settlement_lines, claims)
findings.claim: marketplace columns are unconstrained text, so the acceptance-criterion-4 idempotency key splits on spelling
findings.failure_scenario:
connections.marketplace carries a composite FK to marketplaces(tenant_id, marketplace) (connections_marketplace_fkey, added deliberately at line 388 of the seed migration), but the six other marketplace columns carry no FK and no CHECK, although their comments all read 'One of the six identifiers the marketplaces catalogue defines'. The migration itself says at line 235-236 that '(tenant_id, marketplace) with external_id is the upsert key, which is what makes an ingest run idempotent'. Because marketplace is free text, a connector that emits 'BOL' rather than 'bol' does not collide with the existing row: it creates a second one, and the ingest is silently no longer idempotent. There is also no check that an order's marketplace agrees with its own connection's marketplace.

MEASURED:
All three inserts accepted (INSERT 0 1 each). The select returned three rows for one order id: marketplace = 'bol', 'BOL', 'Bol.com NL', all external_id = 'ORD-9', all on the same connection whose own marketplace is 'bol'. `select conname from pg_constraint where conrelid='public.orders'::regclass and contype='f'` returns only orders_connection_id_fkey and orders_tenant_id_fkey.

findings.file: seen.marketplace_catalogue, row marketplace='bol', capabilities->'buyer_messages'; copied per tenant into public.marketplaces by seen.seed_marketplaces(uuid)
findings.claim: The seeded capability flag for Bol correspondence reads 'out of scope for the MVP' where the routing table says assisted via the inbox
findings.failure_scenario:
Acceptance criterion 5 is that the seed's capability flags match the routing table in docs/architecture.md. Line 21 of that table reads `| Buyer messages and correspondence | none by API (assisted via inbox) | ...`, and the legend three paragraphs above it defines the vocabulary: "'API' means the agent acts end to end; 'assisted' means the agent prepares text, evidence and a deep link and a human submits in one click, after which the agent tracks the outcome; 'none' means out of scope for the MVP." The seed stores mode 'none'. packages/core/db/marketplaces.ts repeats the same definition in its own words ('none' is out of scope for the MVP) and states why the distinction is the point: "Capabilities are stored as the table states them ... and never as booleans: assisted and none are different answers and the claims rail routes on the difference." Bol correspondence is not out of scope: the architecture's own consequence sentence says "Bol is the only marketplace with no messaging API, so its correspondence runs through the tenant's forwarded mailbox", the PRD ships it as Serve (FR-28 names "a Postmark inbound mailbox for Bol with thread matching by order id", FR-29 the drafted replies), and SEEN-062 and SEEN-063 build it in Sprint 5. The stored detail is the tell: it is 'by API (assisted via inbox)', which is the second half of the negation rather than a detail, because the parser's longest-prefix rule took 'none' off the front of 'none by API'. A module reading capabilities->'buyer_messages'->>'mode' for bol is told the capability is out of scope. marketplaces.ts already carries an EXCEPTIONS map for exactly this case, the cells no prefix rule can read, and this cell is not in it.

MEASURED:
The database returns `bol | {"mode": "none", "detail": "by API (assisted via inbox)"}`, against amazon/ebay/kaufland/otto all 'api' and shopify 'n/a'. The document line is `| Buyer messages and correspondence | none by API (assisted via inbox) | API (Messaging, Solicitations) | ...`. The independent round-trip of all 54 cells found the six marketplaces and nine capabilities present and every other cell faithful: the only two other diffs it reported were artefacts of my own reconstruction rule (amazon and bol track_credit, where the documented rule deliberately keeps the brackets because the sentence continues past them) and shopify competing_offers 'own price only', which marketplaces.ts maps by hand in EXCEPTIONS. Note that the repository's own comparison cannot catch this one, because it parses the document with the same parser that produced the seed, so both sides share the reading.

findings.claim: Three externally sourced tables carry a marketplace id with no unique index, so a second ingest of the same page duplicates the rows
findings.failure_scenario:
The ticket description is that "every externally sourced table has a unique index on (tenant_id, marketplace, external_id)", and part 1 states the reason beside the five indexes it does create: "one row per (tenant, marketplace, external id), so reading the same page of a marketplace's API twice writes the row once". Ten columns in public hold a marketplace-assigned id. Five carry the criterion-4 index and listings carries the connection-scoped form of it, `listings_tenant_id_connection_id_external_offer_id_key`, which shows that the author knew how to key a table whose external id is scoped by a parent rather than by a marketplace string. The remaining three have nothing. order_lines has only the primary key on id and `order_lines_tenant_id_id_key`; message_threads has `message_threads_external_thread_id_idx btree (tenant_id, external_thread_id)`, created deliberately and left non-unique; messages has no index on external_message_id at all. order_lines is the row every downstream number hangs off: fee_expectations keys on it one to one, settlement_lines and returns reference it, and margin and headroom are summed from unit_price_cents. So a re-read of an order writes its lines again and the trade record double counts. message_threads and messages are what SEEN-061 ingests from four marketplaces and SEEN-062 parses out of the forwarded mailbox, where redelivery of the same message is ordinary rather than exceptional.

MEASURED:
Every duplicate insert returned `INSERT 0 1`. order_lines: 2 rows for LINE-1, sum(unit_price_cents) = 3998 where the order line is worth 1999 cents. message_threads: 2 rows for THREAD-1. messages: 2 rows for MSG-1. The control was refused: `ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "orders_tenant_marketplace_external_id_key"  DETAIL: Key (tenant_id, marketplace, external_id)=(4444..., bol, ORD-1) already exists.`

findings.file: public.orders.marketplace, and the same column on shipments, returns, settlements and settlement_lines; unique indexes orders_tenant_marketplace_external_id_key and its four siblings
findings.claim: orders.marketplace need not agree with its own connection's marketplace, so the criterion-4 unique index guards only a consistent speller
findings.failure_scenario:
public.connections.marketplace carries a real FK to public.marketplaces(tenant_id, marketplace). None of the five tables named by acceptance criterion 4 does, and none has a check constraint, so the column the uniqueness of an externally sourced row is keyed on is unvalidated free text that can also contradict the connection the row hangs from. The same marketplace order can therefore be stored more than once by varying only the spelling, which is what the index is there to prevent. Part of this is a documented decision (migration part 7 records that status, mode and marketplace are deliberately unconstrained so that "a value nobody anticipated must land in the record and be reconciled, not rejected at ingest"), and that argument covers an unexpected value; it does not cover a row whose marketplace contradicts its own connection_id, which no constraint or trigger checks. Criterion 4 is satisfied as written (all five indexes exist) and this is what it buys.

MEASURED:
All three order inserts succeeded: [{"marketplace":"amazon"},{"marketplace":"bol"},{"marketplace":"Bol"}] all with external_id='DUP-1' on the same bol connection; the unique index never fired. The claims insert with marketplace='not-a-marketplace' and status='banana' also succeeded. For contrast, the genuine key race behaves correctly: two sessions inserting the identical ('bol','RACE-1') give s2 = 23505 duplicate key at read committed, repeatable read and serializable, one row surviving each time.

findings.file: public.order_lines (external_line_id) — supabase/migrations/20260927000000_trade_record_v1_tenancy_and_orders.sql:246-262 and the "Idempotent ingest" block at lines 396-409
findings.claim: order_lines has no uniqueness on its marketplace line id, so re-ingesting one order duplicates every line and no upsert is possible
findings.failure_scenario:
The migration's own heading over the five unique indexes reads "The externally sourced tables: one row per (tenant, marketplace, external id), so reading the same page of a marketplace's API twice writes the row once." order_lines is externally sourced on that same page — its column comment is "Not buyer PII. The marketplace's own line id, which is what a settlement line refers to" — and it is the one externally sourced table in the set with no unique key of any kind on its external identifier. It has a single non-unique index, order_lines_order_id_idx on (order_id). Every other externally sourced table has one: orders/shipments/returns/settlements/settlement_lines on (tenant_id, marketplace, external_id), listings on (tenant_id, connection_id, external_offer_id), products on (tenant_id, sku). The consequence is not only duplicate rows: fee_expectations carries UNIQUE (tenant_id, order_line_id), so a duplicated line forks into two fee expectations that no detector can reconcile; settlement_lines.order_line_id and returns.order_line_id resolve to whichever duplicate the matcher happened to see, which is exactly the deterministic matching SEEN-018 is meant to guarantee; and unit_price_cents and quantity sum to n times the truth after n syncs. SEEN-014 ("idempotent upserts") is blocked by this ticket and cannot write the statement it needs, because ON CONFLICT requires a unique index to arbitrate.

MEASURED:
All three inserts accepted. count=3, qty=3, cents=3000 for one (tenant_id, order_id, external_line_id). The upsert was refused: ERROR: there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification (SQLSTATE 42P10). The index list for order_lines is exactly three entries: order_lines_pkey on (id), order_lines_tenant_id_id_key on (tenant_id, id) — the tenant-scoped FK target, not a business key — and order_lines_order_id_idx on (order_id), which is not unique.

findings.file: public.orders.marketplace, shipments.marketplace, returns.marketplace, settlements.marketplace, settlement_lines.marketplace, claims.marketplace; contrast public.connections.marketplace — supabase/migrations/20260927000002_trade_record_v1_commerce_and_marketplaces_seed.sql:403-405
findings.claim: Six of the seven marketplace columns are unconstrained free text although each says it is one of the six catalogue identifiers, and criterion 4's unique index inherits that weakness
findings.failure_scenario:
All seven marketplace columns carry the identical comment "Not buyer PII. One of the six identifiers the marketplaces catalogue defines." Exactly one of them enforces it: connections_marketplace_fkey, FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, marketplace) REFERENCES marketplaces(tenant_id, marketplace) ON UPDATE CASCADE. The other six accept any text. That is not the value-set constraint part 2 declines on principle (so an unanticipated value lands rather than being rejected) — it is the catalogue key, and the schema already applies precisely this tenant-scoped foreign key to it one table over. Two concrete consequences. First, criterion 4's unique index on (tenant_id, marketplace, external_id) is the ingest idempotency key, and a marketplace string that varies by spelling makes the same marketplace order a second row straight past it, which is the guarantee the index was created for. Second, orders.marketplace is denormalised beside connection_id and nothing ties the two together, so an order can be recorded against a Bol connection while claiming to be an Amazon order, and a settlement line can claim a different marketplace from the settlement it hangs under — with fee expectations, detectors and the claims rail all routed by that column.

MEASURED:
The control was refused: ERROR: insert or update on table "connections" violates foreign key constraint "connections_marketplace_fkey", DETAIL: Key (tenant_id, marketplace)=(..., not-a-marketplace) is not present in table "marketplaces" (23503). Every other insert was accepted. orders for tenant :ta afterwards: (ORD-1, bol, bol), (ORD-1, Bol, bol), (ORD-1, not-a-marketplace, bol), (ORD-2, amazon, bol) — three rows for one external order id inside one tenant, past orders_tenant_marketplace_external_id_key, and one order on a bol connection recorded as amazon. settlement_lines: line_mk=amazon under settlement_mk=bol, accepted.

findings.file: public.evidence (evidence_tenant_id_fkey ON DELETE CASCADE) and the storage.objects rows of the `evidence` bucket created by supabase/migrations/20260924000000_evidence_bucket.sql
findings.claim: Erasing a tenant deletes the pointer to its evidence and leaves the bytes in the bucket, with the only tenant mapping destroyed by the same statement
findings.failure_scenario:
The eight-migration set gives every one of the 29 public tables a tenant_id, an RLS policy and an ON DELETE CASCADE to tenants, and adds seen.erased_tenants so an erased id can never be reissued. None of that reaches the storage bucket. public.evidence.storage_path is the only thing in the database that says which stored object belongs to which tenant, and it is deleted by the very cascade that is supposed to carry out the erasure. After `delete from public.tenants`, the tenant's evidence rows are gone, its objects are still in the `evidence` bucket, and there is no longer any row anywhere that associates those objects with the erased tenant. The bucket migration's own comment says an evidence object 'is a buyer's document as often as it is an invoice', and evidence.buyer_name/buyer_address carry the comment 'Written only as far as a claim needs it and expired after 30 days by SEEN-083' - a story the columns have and the files do not. storage.objects has RLS enabled with zero policies and no tenant column, so nothing else can reconstruct the mapping. This contradicts the ground rule 'delete tenants on request' and the buyer-PII expiry rule, and it is unrecoverable after the fact rather than merely incomplete: a later SEEN-083 job has nothing left to join on.

MEASURED:
before: evidence=2 objects=2 / after : evidence=0 objects=2. Both files still listed after the erasure, including 'aaaaaaaa-0000-0000-0000-000000000001/claims/x/carrier-proof.pdf', while seen.erased_tenants recorded aaaaaaaa-0000-0000-0000-000000000001 as erased. storage.objects: relrowsecurity=true with zero rows in pg_policies for schemaname='storage'.

findings.claim: evidence.storage_path is free text with no relation to evidence.tenant_id, so a row inside one tenant's RLS boundary can point at another tenant's stored document
findings.failure_scenario:
Part 5 of the schema rewrote every parent link as (tenant_id, child_id) references parent (tenant_id, id) precisely so that a row cannot reach across the tenant boundary through a foreign key, and it works: the tenant-scoped evidence_claim_id_fkey refused my first attempt to attach tenant B's claim_id to a tenant A evidence row with 23503. But the column that actually addresses the buyer's document is a bare text field with no check, no prefix constraint and no relation to the row's own tenant_id, and storage.objects has no tenant column and no policy to compensate. So an evidence row that passes the tenant_isolation policy for tenant A, and is returned to an authenticated tenant A session, can name a path under tenant B's prefix; the application then resolves it to a signed URL over tenant B's buyer invoice. The tenant boundary that 29 tables enforce stops at the pointer. This matters more than a generic free-text complaint because evidence assembly is a model-driven step (the agent assembles the case pack) and the storage path is exactly the kind of value the policy gate is meant to constrain, yet the database accepts any string. A check tying storage_path to tenant_id::text||'/' would close it with the technique the schema already uses elsewhere.

MEASURED:
INSERT 0 1, accepted. Row: evidence_owner=aaaaaaaa-0000-0000-0000-000000000001, storage_path=bbbbbbbb-0000-0000-0000-000000000002/claims/secret/buyer-invoice.pdf. The contrasting attempt that crossed tenants via claim_id was refused: 'insert or update on table "evidence" violates foreign key constraint "evidence_claim_id_fkey"'.

findings.file: constraint connections_marketplace_fkey on public.connections, FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, marketplace) REFERENCES public.marketplaces (tenant_id, marketplace) ON UPDATE CASCADE (supabase/migrations/20260927000002_trade_record_v1_commerce_and_marketplaces_seed.sql:402-406)
findings.claim: connections_marketplace_fkey cascades on both columns of its key, so one UPDATE of public.marketplaces.tenant_id silently moves another tenant's connection and its credential reference
findings.failure_scenario:
The migration states the intent beside the constraint: 'on update cascade so renaming an identifier in the catalogue carries the connections with it rather than orphaning them.' That reasoning covers one column of the key. The constraint is on the composite (tenant_id, marketplace), so the cascade fires on a change to either column, and a change to marketplaces.tenant_id rewrites connections.tenant_id. The rewrite is a referential action: it does not pass through the connections RLS policy, and connections has no trigger that would object. seen.refuse_tenant_id_change exists on exactly one table, public.tenants, where its own error text says a tenant id 'is the identity twenty-eight tables reference' - and the one place the schema moves a tenant_id by itself is not guarded. What moves is not an ordinary row: connections carries credential_ref, the Secret Manager pointer for that seller account, plus scopes and external_seller_id. Reachable only by a role that can write public.marketplaces, which is service_role or postgres, not authenticated - so this is a defence-in-depth gap rather than a client-reachable one, but service_role is what apps/api and apps/worker run as, and a single wrong UPDATE in the marketplaces-maintenance path hands one tenant another tenant's marketplace credentials with no audit event and no error.

MEASURED:
Before: tenant_id=aaaaaaaa-0000-0000-0000-000000000001 | bol | projects/seen/secrets/tenantA-bol-oauth. After UPDATE 1 on public.marketplaces: tenant_id=bbbbbbbb-0000-0000-0000-000000000002 | bol | projects/seen/secrets/tenantA-bol-oauth. No error, no trigger fired that objected.

findings.file: public.invoices.recovery_share_lines jsonb not null default '[]'::jsonb (supabase/migrations/20260927000002_trade_record_v1_commerce_and_marketplaces_seed.sql:128) and public.invoices.total_cents
findings.claim: The billable-event chain has no last hop: invoices.recovery_share_lines is untyped jsonb, so a recovery share can be billed against a claim that was never credited, does not exist, or has already been billed
findings.failure_scenario:
The ground rule is that a credit is billable only as an ingested settlement line linked to a claim, and that neither a person nor the agent may create a billable event directly; the architecture's seventh principle says 'the meter and the ledger are the same table'. The schema builds the chain carefully up to the second-last link - settlement_lines is ingested, and claims.credited_by_settlement_line_id is a real tenant-scoped composite foreign key to settlement_lines (tenant_id, id). Then it stops. The column that turns a credited claim into money the company charges is a jsonb array with a default of '[]', no foreign key, no check constraint, and no counterpart marker on claims saying a claim has been invoiced. Its own comment states the contract the database does not enforce: 'One entry per credited claim: the claim id, the credited amount and the share charged on it.' Nothing checks that the cited claim exists, belongs to the same tenant, is at status 'credited', or carries a non-null credited_by_settlement_line_id; nothing stops the same claim appearing on two invoices; and total_cents bears no declared relation to the lines. The contrast inside the same schema is the tell: headroom_entries, the other meter, has a tenant-scoped FK to price_changes (tenant_id, id) and a unique key on (tenant_id, price_change_id, counted_on). The revenue meter has neither. SEEN-040 is specified as 'Issue invoices with recovery-share lines from credited claims only', and this ticket hands it a column in which that sentence is unrepresentable.

MEASURED:
Both inserts accepted (INSERT 0 1 each). Resulting rows: total_cents=2500000 with 1 line, and total_cents=9900000 with 2 lines, i.e. EUR 124,000 of recovery share billed at status 'open' against one claim still at status 'draft' with a null credit link, one line of which cites a claim id present in no table. The claim row throughout: status=draft, credited_by_settlement_line_id=(null).
